tweets.text:
After launching on Aug. 30, @NASARoman is on its way to its final destination, where it will change how we view the universe.
 
You can adopt a pixel in one of Roman's first images, expected by early 2027. Sign up today to claim yours: https://go.nasa.gov/AdoptAPixel https://x.com/NASA/status/2098078917751951729/photo/1

media.altText: A black-and-white infrared view of a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket as it lifts off into the sky with the Roman Space Telescope aboard. The background sky is dark and fluffy, gray clouds mark the bottom of the photo. The rocket and its trail glow bright white in the center of the photo. Credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky
A certificate that is granted upon adopting a pixel in one of the first images taken by the Roman Space Telescope. This certificate is addressed to Nancy Roman. Credit: NASA

tweets.text:
Today, @NASADepAdmin and I hosted the first meeting of the Commission on the United States Space Academy. We were honored to welcome @SecWar, @SecAFOfficial, and leaders from @NASA, @WHOMB, @WHOSTP47, @WhiteHouse and across the Administration to @NASA Headquarters.

Under https://t.co/7YQ7sOTJ54

retweetedTweet.text:
Today, @NASADepAdmin and I hosted the first meeting of the Commission on the United States Space Academy. We were honored to welcome @SecWar, @SecAFOfficial, and leaders from @NASA, @WHOMB, @WHOSTP47, @WhiteHouse and across the Administration to @NASA Headquarters.

Under President Trump’s leadership, the Artemis Program, Artemis Accords, and Space Force were established, and soon there will be a prestigious United States Space Academy to help ensure American leadership in space by developing the talent necessary to advance our national security, scientific, and economic interests across the great frontier.

author.bio: Serving President Donald J. Trump as the 15th @NASA Administrator | Leading the next Golden Age of space discovery 🚀

I’ve known Reid and Victor for years, and I’m grateful for everything they have given to NASA, including helping return America to the lunar environment on Artemis II.

I’m especially glad that service is continuing.

Through the emeritus program, they’ll keep mentoring astronauts, flight controllers, and engineers and passing along the experience that will help make Artemis III and the missions that follow stronger.

Thank you both for everything you’ve done, and everything you’ll keep doing.

Meir was attached to an articulating portable foot restraint installed on Canadarm2’s latching end effector. The orbital outpost was soaring 259 miles above the Pacific Ocean southwest of Mexico when this photograph was taken.
